title: Design Memory Allocator
description:
# Design Memory Allocator

You are given an integer `n`, the size of a 0-indexed memory array. Every memory unit is initially free.

Implement the `Allocator` class:

* `Allocator(int n)` initializes the allocator with `n` free memory units.
* `int allocate(int size, int mID)` finds the leftmost block of `size` consecutive free memory units, marks every unit in that block as belonging to `mID`, and returns the block's leftmost index. If no such block exists, return `-1` and do not change memory.
* `int free(int mID)` frees every memory unit currently assigned to `mID` and returns the number of units freed. If `mID` owns no memory, return `0`.

The same `mID` may receive multiple separate allocations. A later `free(mID)` must release all of them. Allocation is strict first-fit: even if a larger block exists later, the allocator must choose the earliest block that can fit `size` consecutive units.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["Allocator", "allocate", "allocate", "allocate", "free", "allocate", "allocate", "allocate", "free", "allocate", "free"]
[[10], [1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2], [3, 4], [1, 1], [1, 1], [1], [10, 2], [7]]

**Output:**
[null, 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 6, 3, -1, 0]

**Explanation:**
The first three one-unit allocations occupy indices `0`, `1`, and `2`. Freeing `mID = 2` releases index `1`. The next size-3 allocation cannot fit at index `1`, so it starts at index `3`. Later `mID = 1` owns indices `0`, `1`, and `6`; `free(1)` releases all three units.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= n, size, mID <= 1000`
* At most `1000` calls will be made to `allocate` and `free`.

diagrams.caption: First-fit allocation over freed memory ranges

solutions.name: Direct Cell Array First Fit
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store the owner `mID` in each memory cell, using `0` for free cells. Allocation scans left to right while counting the current free run. When the run reaches `size`, fill exactly that block with `mID`. Freeing scans the whole array and clears every matching cell.

## Key Insight

This is the clearest model of the prompt: first-fit means the first run of zeros with enough length. It also makes the rule that one `mID` may own several separate blocks easy to verify, because `free` removes every matching cell.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n) for allocation and O(n) for free.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the memory owner array.

solutions.name: BitSet Free Run Search
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n / word + k) per allocate, O(n) per free
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a `BitSet` to record which cells are occupied and an owner array to remember the `mID` of each occupied unit. Allocation jumps from one clear run to the next with `nextClearBit` and `nextSetBit`, then marks the chosen range. Freeing clears the occupied bits whose owner matches the requested id.

## Key Insight

A bitset keeps the same first-fit semantics as the array baseline, but it teaches a compact representation of free and used cells. Jumping across occupied stretches also prevents the allocation loop from checking every cell in dense memory.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n / word + k) for allocation in typical bitset scanning, where k is the allocated range length, and O(n) for free.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the owner array and occupancy bits.

solutions.name: Allocated Interval TreeMap
solutions.timeComplexity: O(b log b) allocate, O(r log b) free
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store only allocated blocks in a `TreeMap` ordered by start index. Allocation scans the gaps before and between allocated blocks to find the earliest gap with enough length. A second map records the block starts owned by each `mID`, so `free(mID)` can remove every matching interval.

## Key Insight

Instead of remembering free space directly, the allocator can derive free gaps from allocated intervals. This is a useful design route when the number of blocks is much smaller than the memory size.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(b log b) to scan and insert among b allocated blocks, and O(r log b) to free r blocks owned by the id.
- Space Complexity: O(b) for allocated block records and id-to-block indexes.

solutions.name: TreeMap Free Intervals with Coalescing
solutions.timeComplexity: O(f log f + r log f) per operation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain free memory as sorted half-open intervals in a `TreeMap`, and keep allocated ranges grouped by `mID`. Allocation scans free intervals in order and consumes the left edge of the first interval with enough space. Freeing returns every range for the id and coalesces it with adjacent free intervals.

## Key Insight

This route models the allocator as a free-list, which is how many real allocators are explained. Coalescing adjacent free ranges is the important invariant: without it, a later large allocation might fail even though enough contiguous memory was restored.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(f log f) to find and update among f free intervals, plus O(r log f) when freeing r ranges.
- Space Complexity: O(f + b), for free intervals and allocated block records.

solutions.name: Segment Tree Leftmost Free Block
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) allocate range update plus O(r log n) free
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a segment tree where each node stores the longest free prefix, longest free suffix, and longest free block in its range. Allocation descends to the leftmost segment whose best free run can fit `size`, marks that range as occupied, and records it under `mID`. Freeing replays range assignments to make every owned range free again.

## Key Insight

First-fit can be answered without scanning every cell if each interval knows enough summary information. The `left.suffix + right.prefix` case is what detects a free block crossing the midpoint while still returning the leftmost valid start.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n) to find and allocate one block, and O(r log n) to free r ranges owned by the id.
- Space Complexity: O(n + b) for the segment tree and recorded allocations.

tests.description: Canonical sample with first-fit reuse, repeated mID allocations, and failed large allocation.
First-fit allocation after fragmented frees and reused mIDs.
One mID may own multiple non-adjacent blocks, and free(mID) releases all of them before coalescing.
Exact full-memory allocation, failed allocation while full, missing free, and reuse after freeing everything.
When two holes fit, allocation must choose the leftmost fitting hole, not a later or larger one.
Repeated free on the same mID must return zero after the first release.
Separate holes cannot be combined unless the blocking allocation between them is also freed.
Single-cell memory still obeys failed allocation, successful free, and reuse semantics.
